title: One-colour brioche
sourceNotes: One-colour brioche stitch is a traditional technique found in Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s) and widely described in Mary Thomas, Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938). Out of copyright UK/EU. Modern brioche abbreviations (brk, brp, sl1yo) are now industry-standard per Craft Yarn Council conventions.

glossaryTerms.definition: A knitting technique in which each stitch is slipped with a yarn over on one row and worked together with that yarn over on the next, producing a tall, deeply-ribbed reversible fabric.
A length of smooth yarn or thread threaded through all live stitches at a checkpoint row, allowing the knitter to rip back to that row safely if a mistake is found later.

content.text: The secret of one-colour
brioche

is that every stitch is worked over two rows, not one. On the first pass, the stitch is slipped with a yarn over. On the second pass, the slip and yarn over are worked together. This is a brioche knit (brk) on the knit side and a brioche purl (brp) on the purl side. The result is the tall, squishy columns that give the fabric its character.

You need yarn and needles. Work in a smooth dk or aran weight yarn to learn the rhythm before tackling finer weights. The fabric grows half as quickly as stocking stitch because each stitch takes two passes.
Step by step

Abbreviations used: brk = brioche knit; brp = brioche purl; sl1yo = slip 1 stitch purlwise with yarn in front, then take the yarn over the needle to the back. This creates the slip and the yarn over in one move.
Cast on an odd number of stitches. Row 1 (set-up, worked once only): *k1, sl1yo; repeat from * to last stitch, k1.
Row 2 (brioche row A): *brk1 (knit the slipped stitch together with its yarn over), sl1yo; repeat from * to last stitch, brk1.
Row 3 (brioche row B): *sl1yo, brp1 (purl the slipped stitch together with its yarn over); repeat from * to last stitch, sl1yo. End k1 if working flat with a selvedge stitch.
Repeat rows 2 and 3 for the fabric. The two-row repeat is the complete brioche cycle.
To cast off, work a standard cast-off but note that each brk stitch counts as 1 stitch, not 2, so the stitch count on the needle feels halved compared with a standard fabric.
Where you'll see it

One-colour brioche produces the classic reversible rib-like fabric used for cowls, scarves, and hat brims where the same face reads from both sides. It is also the foundation stitch for two-colour brioche, which adds a second yarn colour to each of the two brioche rows.
Common faults

Accidental increases from double yarn overs. The sl1yo must be one slip plus one yarn over, not two yarn overs. Check that the yarn is taken forward before slipping the stitch and then taken over the needle, not wrapped a second time.

Stitch count halving or doubling unexpectedly. Brioche stitches on the needle look like two loops sitting together; counting them as two rather than one inflates the count. Count only the brk stitches (the paired loop) as one stitch each.
Missed yarn over produces a hole and a decrease. If the yarn over is skipped on the sl1yo, the following brk works the slip alone, leaving a hole, and the stitch count drops by 1. Place a
lifeline
every 20 rows while learning.
What to try next: once brioche feels easy, move on to
two-colour brioche
. It uses the same brk and brp actions with two alternating yarn colours to make the shadow-rib effect.
